items.title: Forged in the Arctic, Built for the Fight: 11th Airborne Division Trains Across Pacific
items.author: Correy Mathews
items.summary: The 11th Airborne Division is demonstrating its ability to operate across the Pacific while maintaining its Arctic responsibilities in Alaska. Nearly simultaneous participation in Yama Sakura 91 and Orient Shield 26 in Japan, Yudh Abhyas 2026 in India, and Super Garuda Shield 26 in Indonesia places Arctic Angels alongside key allies and partners in environments ranging from mountains and jungles to complex command and control exercises. The division’s Arctic training prepares Soldiers to operate
items.body:
Joint Base Elmendorf–Richardson, Alaska — The 11th Airborne Division is forged in the Arctic, but its battlefield extends far beyond Alaska. Across the Pacific, Arctic Angels are training nearly simultaneously during Yama Sakura 91 and Orient Shield 26 in Japan, Yudh Abhyas 2026 in India, and Super Garuda Shield 26 in Indonesia. Separated by thousands of miles, the exercises place 11th Airborne Division Soldiers in different terrain, climates and formations alongside some of the United States’ closest allies and partners, all with a common purpose: build combat ready forces capable of moving, integrating and fighting together when required.

“The Arctic is our expertise, but it is not our limitation,” said Maj. Gen. John P. Cogbill, commanding general, 11th Airborne Division. “What you see across the Pacific is a division demonstrating that it can move forces across the theater, integrate with our allies and partners and remain ready to fight wherever the mission demands. From Alaska to Japan, India and Indonesia, our Soldiers are proving the reach, readiness and lethality this division brings to the region.”

Alaska is where that capability is forged. Extreme cold, isolation, limited infrastructure and vast distances leave little room for weakness. Soldiers must be able to survive, communicate, sustain themselves and accomplish the mission when the environment is actively working against them. That training produces formations accustomed to operating under pressure, solving problems with limited resources and continuing the mission when conditions deteriorate. The temperature and terrain may change across the Pacific, but the requirement for leaders to be engaged and build lethal formations does not.

In Indonesia, 11th Airborne Division Soldiers participating in Super Garuda Shield 26 are training alongside the Indonesian National Armed Forces and multinational partners. The exercise includes jungle training, a partnered joint forcible entry operation and follow on field training designed to increase the ability of participating forces to operate as a combined team. The dense vegetation, heat and humidity create a problem set far removed from the Arctic, but they demand the same fundamentals: understand the terrain, maintain communications, sustain the force and preserve momentum against an opposing force.

In India, Arctic Angels are training alongside the Indian Army during Yudh Abhyas 2026. The bilateral exercise strengthens the ability of U.S. and Indian forces to operate together in demanding environments while building upon the partnership reinforced during Yudh Abhyas 2025 in Alaska. Mountainous and austere terrain places additional demands on Soldiers and leaders, requiring formations capable of adapting quickly, sustaining combat power and continuing operations when normal advantages become difficult to maintain.

“We optimize to train in the extreme cold, high latitude, mountainous terrain and by operating in the harshest environment in the world,” said Command Sgt. Maj. David P. Hanson, command sergeant major, 11th Airborne Division. “We can operate anywhere in the Pacific.”

At the same time, 11th Airborne Division Soldiers in Japan are strengthening the command-and- control and interoperability required for combined operations. During Yama Sakura 91, Soldiers are working alongside the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force and Australian Army during a trilateral command post exercise focused on the ability to plan, synchronize and command forces across a complex battlefield. The exercise requires staff from three nations to overcome differences in doctrine, terminology, systems and processes in order to build the shared understanding required to make decisions and synchronize effects at the speed of combat.

Following the conclusion of Yama Sakura 91, 11th Airborne Division Soldiers will transition into Orient Shield 26, continuing bilateral training with the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force. The exercise will provide another opportunity to strengthen U.S.-Japan warfighting capability and build upon the relationships, systems and interoperability developed through repeated training together. While Yama Sakura focuses on trilateral command-and-control alongside Japanese and Australian forces, Orient Shield will continue the division’s progression of training in Japan and reinforce the ability of U.S. and Japanese forces to operate together in competition, crisis or conflict.

The scale of the division’s participation across the Pacific is itself a demonstration of readiness. The 11th Airborne Division is not concentrating its forces on a single training area, exercise or mission. Elements of the formation are operating across multiple countries and environments during the same training period while the division continues to maintain forces and responsibilities in Alaska. In a theater defined by immense distances, that ability to operate distributed requires forces that can deploy, sustain themselves, communicate across distance, integrate with partners and remain capable of closing with and defeating an enemy.

The Arctic prepares Soldiers for that kind of fight. Alaska forces Soldiers and leaders to operate when equipment is stressed, movement is difficult, resources are limited and the environment punishes mistakes. Those conditions build disciplined formations that understand how to maintain combat power when circumstances are at their worst. When Arctic Angels leave Alaska, they carry those lessons with them.

From the Arctic to the mountains of India, the jungles of Indonesia and training areas across Japan, the 11th Airborne Division is demonstrating that its Soldiers are not defined by a single environment. The Arctic is where they are forged. The Pacific is where they prove that capability can translate anywhere the mission demands.

items.title: Naval Medical Forces Pacific and Japanese delegation expand bilateral maritime medicine cooperation
items.author: Arsenio R. Cortez Jr.
items.summary: Naval Medical Forces Pacific hosted a senior delegation of Japanese government and officials, clinical leaders and academic researchers Aug. 25, 2026, to deepen bilateral medical collaboration and examine the operational requirements of maritime healthcare across the vast Indo-Pacific region.
items.body:
Naval Medical Forces Pacific hosted a senior delegation of Japanese government and officials, clinical leaders and academic researchers Aug. 25, 2026, to deepen bilateral medical collaboration and examine the operational requirements of maritime healthcare across the vast Indo-Pacific region. Led by Jun Tsushima, state minister of the Cabinet Office of Japan, the delegation met with NMFP leadership to exchange expertise on shipboard medical doctrine, underway clinical training, emergency response integration and the future architecture of afloat hospital platforms. Rear Adm. Kevin Brown, commander of NMFP and director of Defense Health Network-Pacific Rim, provided the delegates with an overview of the command’s expansive area of responsibility. Central to the command’s mission is the preparation and sustainment of a ready medical force capable of rapidly mobilizing from shore to operational theaters, including deployments aboard the hospital ship USNS Mercy. "The vast majority of our doctors, nurses, corpsmen and clinical support specialists work daily within our shore hospitals and clinics delivering routine patient care,” Brown said. “When a crisis emerges and the USNS Mercy receives operational tasking, we draw those ready deployable medical teams from our medical treatment facilities to perform life-saving care in theater while keeping our military treatment facilities prepared to receive returning casualties.” For Japanese leadership, cultivating maritime medical capability represents both an urgent humanitarian requirement and a vital defense priority. Tsushima explained that while Japan's health care system is highly effective in executing medical responses on land, its experience in delivering care at sea remains limited. Because Japan is surrounded by water and frequently impacted by natural disasters such as earthquakes, tsunamis and typhoons, he emphasized the critical importance of developing shipboard medical capabilities to support emergency care. During the discussion, delegates explored the operational trade-offs between large floating hospitals and smaller, specialized vessels. Brown outlined current U.S. Navy modernization concepts, highlighting the ongoing requirement for agile, shallow-draft platforms capable of delivering Role 2 damage-control resuscitation and stabilization close to contested waters, alongside future long-term planning to replace aging 1980s-era converted tanker hospital ships with modern Role 3 afloat medical capabilities. Addressing questions from Yoichi Koida of the Japan Institute for Health Security, Brown noted that the strategic geography of the Pacific dictates the evolution in combat casualty care and medical evacuation doctrine. "Over the past 30 years, our ability to move life-saving surgical teams near the point of injury and evacuate casualties through an uncontested medical evacuation system was the greatest contributor to combat survival rates," Brown explained. "However, in a conflict across the Pacific, we might not always have the luxury of uninterrupted command of the air and sea, or continuous electronic communications. Planners are exploring various concepts, including leveraging highly mobile, agile afloat medical platforms capable of delivering immediate damage-control surgery in communications-suppressed environments." Clinical workflow was also a central focus of the exchange. John Rotruck, chief medical officer for Defense Health Network-Pacific Rim, highlighted essential design lessons from current operations, recommending that future hospital ship configurations maintain casualty receiving, trauma resuscitation, advanced radiology, surgical suites and intensive care units on the same deck to eliminate vertical patient transport for critically injured individuals. “Keeping all the most critical parts of the care pathway on the same deck of the ship allows a natural flow of care,” Rotruck said. Brown also emphasized the Pacific Partnership mission as a proven framework for ongoing coordination between military planners, civilian medical systems and partner nations, recommending Japanese participation in early-stage joint planning cells. Concluding the exchange, Tsushima expressed strong interest in expanding future bilateral cooperation between the United States and Japan across maritime medical response missions. He emphasized that growing opportunities for joint training, sharing operational experience, and learning from each other will ensure both nations are better prepared to preserve life during natural disasters and complex emergencies. NMFP provides oversight for 10 Navy Medicine Readiness and Training Commands (NMRTC) on the West Coast and Pacific Rim that train, man and equip medical forces, primarily in military treatment facilities. Globally, NMFP oversees eight research laboratories that deliver research expertise in support of warfighter health and readiness. Additionally, NMFP manages the Naval Expeditionary Medicine Warfighter Development Center (NEMWDC), which plays a critical role in preparing medical teams for expeditionary and operational environments.

items.title: TEMPORARY FLIGHT RESTRICTIONS ANNOUNCED OVER BEDMINSTER, NEW JERSEY THIS WEEKEND
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: The North American Aerospace Defense Command will enforce multiple VIP Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR) areas established by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) over the New Jersey area this long weekend, with impacts to general aviation September 4 - 7, 2026.
items.body:
TYNDALL AIR FORCE BASE, Fla. – The North American Aerospace Defense Command will enforce multiple VIP Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR) areas established by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) over the New Jersey area this long weekend, with impacts to general aviation September 4 - 7, 2026. General aviation pilots are reminded to check Notices to Airmen, or NOTAMs, before each flight as required by the FAA, and TFR procedures must be followed. If required, NORAD aircraft will respond to aircraft violating TFRs and take the necessary action to gain compliance – a scenario we encourage all pilots to avoid. Pilots can access the most up-to-date information published by the FAA at https://tfr.faa.gov/ Pilots and the public may also notice U.S. Army ground-based air defense equipment in the same geographic region. These systems are operating under NORAD authorities, constitute a routine component of the command’s layered defense posture and work in tandem with the command’s airborne assets to monitor and protect the airspace. NORAD employs a layered defense network of radars, satellites, fighter aircraft, and other capabilities to identify and respond to potential threats. This defense posture demonstrates how NORAD executes Operation NOBLE EAGLE - its vital aerospace warning and control mission for North America. For more information about General Aviation and TFRs visit https://www.norad.mil/General-Aviation/

items.title: From Baghdad to the Fleet: Marine Recruiter Enlists His Own Replacement
items.author: Sgt Tanner Pittard
items.summary: After growing up in war-torn Baghdad inspired by patrolling U.S. service members, Sgt. Hasanein Alrushdawi immigrated to America and walked into a Florida recruiting office in 2022, where he met Gunnery Sgt. Jonathan Carter, a mentor who lived by the philosophy that recruiters don't just write contracts, they enlist their replacements. Carter guided Alrushdawi through recruit training, fleet service, and career milestones, forging a brotherly bond that came full circle in 2024 when Alrushdawi re
items.body:
The Replacement TAMPA, Fla. — In 2001, U.S. Marine Corps Sgt. Hasanein Alrushdawi was born in Baghdad, Iraq. Growing up during a period of intense conflict, his early years were marked by the realities of war. Yet amidst the instability of his homeland, Alrushdawi found inspiration in the U.S. Marines patrolling his neighborhood. "What was always in front of me is United States Marines roaming the streets of my home and I idolized them because they were sacrificing so much for people, they do not even know," Alrushdawi said. He decided at a young age that he wanted to become a selfless protector and earn the title of Marine. Meanwhile, thousands of miles away in the United States, U.S. Marine Corps Gunnery Sgt. Jonathan Carter was seeking his own path. He did not grow up around the Marine Corps or come from a military family, but he possessed an innate desire to help others and challenge himself. "If I knew I was going to join the military, why would I not enlist into the most challenging branch?" Carter said. "My 'why' was always to help others and to make myself and those I love proud." Though they came from completely different backgrounds, their paths would eventually cross in a central Florida recruiting office. By 2012, Alrushdawi’s family had immigrated to the United States. He carried with him a deep, burning sense of gratitude; a debt he felt he owed to the nation that had adopted him. Ten years later, in 2022, he walked into Permanent Contact Station Winter Park, Recruiting Sub-Station Orlando, Recruiting Station Tampa. Behind the desk sat Carter, a seasoned Marine who had volunteered for recruiting duty to make a tangible difference in the lives of young American men and women. Carter was the embodiment of what civilians picture when they think of a Marine: disciplined, compassionate, and intensely focused. When Carter looked at young “Al” standing before him, he didn't just see another applicant to sign up. He saw a "heavy hitter." He saw a young man with a ruthless, natural drive that the Marine Corps didn't forge, but could certainly sharpen into a proud and motivated Marine. For Alrushdawi, looking at Carter brought back an immediate rush of memories from the streets of Baghdad. "He genuinely cared," Alrushdawi recalls. "He wanted to help, but he also gave me a challenge. From that moment, I knew I could never let him down. Failing was never an option." In the Marine Corps, those waiting to go to recruit training are called "poolees." During this critical phase, Carter became more than a recruiter to Alrushdawi; he became a compass. There is an old, cynical saying in sales organizations: Once the contract is signed, the job is done. But the Marine Corps is not a sales organization. "Recruiters don’t write contracts," Carter said. "They enlist their replacements." This philosophy transformed a professional duty into a lifelong brotherhood. Long after Alrushdawi completed Marine Corps recruit training, earned the coveted title of Marine, and went out into the fleet, the phone calls never stopped. Whenever Alrushdawi faced a crossroad, a leadership challenge, or a personal doubt, he dialed the man who had helped him start his journey. And no matter where he was, Carter always answered. "He knows me better than I know myself sometimes," Alrushdawi says. "He became like the older brother I never had." To Carter, watching Alrushdawi grow was the ultimate validation of his career. "I won't let him fail," Carter says simply. In a changing Marine Corps, where recruiters navigate new technologies, shifting generations, and the aftermath of a global pandemic, the one constant is the human element; The enduring professional relationship between a Marine and their mentor. By 2024, Alrushdawi was at a pivotal moment in his career. He was preparing his reenlistment package, having been accepted into the Command Retention Program. He stood at the edge of a new horizon and, naturally, he called his mentor. Alrushdawi asked Carter if he should wait to volunteer for recruiting duty or take the leap immediately. Carter didn't hesitate. He gave his younger brother-in-arms the kind of blunt, direct advice only a true mentor can offer: "Get your ass out here now,” urged Carter. Today, both Marines are back in Florida, working side by side. Alrushdawi, a Marine Corps recruiter in Recruiting Sub-Station Brandon, and Carter the assistant recruiting instructor for Recruiting Station Tampa. The dynamic has shifted yet remained entirely the same. The recruiter and the recruit are now serving side-by-side as fellow Marines, fighting the same battle on the home front and seeking out the next generation of leaders to replace them. For Alrushdawi, the mission is deeply personal. He wants to be the "gatekeeper" for his community, ensuring that only the most qualified, driven young men and women have the opportunity to earn the title Marine. He wants to give others the same life-changing opportunity Carter gave him. For Carter, seeing Alrushdawi back on recruiting duty brings their journey full circle. "This is how we build the best Marine Corps we’ve ever seen," Carter says. "Never lose sight of the importance of what we do." To a civilian, the Marine Corps can look like an impenetrable wall of starch, brass, and rigid protocols. But to those who wear the uniform, the true strength of the Corps lies in its vulnerability: the shared sweat, the collective sacrifice and the unspoken promise that your background matters far less than the direction you are marching. One brother came from the quiet, structured pursuit of an American challenge. The other came from the smoke and rubble of a war zone halfway across the globe. Yet, today, they stand shoulder-to-shoulder in the Florida heat, bound by a promise made years ago in a recruiting office. They are proof that the Marine Corps doesn't just make Marines; it builds a family. It fosters a brotherhood that spans oceans, outlasts contracts, and endures for a lifetime.

items.title: Marine Barracks Washington Guard Marines Awarded for Decisive Action at 8th & I
items.author: CPT Lauri Schleicher
items.summary: WASHINGTON — Five Guard Company Marines assigned to Marine Barracks Washington were recognized for their disciplined and decisive response after an armed individual pointed a weapon toward a guard post outside the installation. Lance Cpl. Joshua Aikman, Lance Cpl. Anthony Verastegui, Lance Cpl. Caden Phillips, Lance Cpl. Logan Carpenter, and Cpl. Ian Caudy relied on their training, one another and the standards expected of Marines to quickly respond, communicate and gain control of the situation
items.body:
WASHINGTON — Five Guard Company Marines assigned to Marine Barracks Washington were recognized for their disciplined and decisive response after an armed individual pointed a weapon toward a guard post outside the installation.

Lance Cpl. Joshua Aikman, Lance Cpl. Anthony Verastegui, Lance Cpl. Caden Phillips, Lance Cpl. Logan Carpenter, and Cpl. Ian Caudy relied on their training, one another and the standards expected of Marines to quickly respond, communicate and gain control of the situation while protecting the Barracks and surrounding community. Their actions reflected the discipline required to perform under pressure and the steady character that allows Marines to exercise sound judgement when circumstances vary from the plan.

“There wasn’t time to think about anything except what we had been trained to do,” Aikman said. “Everyone knew their responsibility, communicated and stayed composed. The goal was to control the situation without anyone getting hurt. Trusting the Marine to your left and right goes a long way in a real-world situation like this.”

Col. Jason C. Copeland, commanding officer of Marine Barracks Washington, presented the five Marines with Navy and Marine Corps Achievement Medals in recognition of their actions. The awards recognized the Marines’ actions as well as the preparation, control, and trust that enabled them to act with composure when it mattered.

Aikman’s parents, Rhonda and Kevin Aikman, traveled from Louisiana to attend the ceremony, underscoring the role Marine families play in the development and success of the force. “Recognizing deserving Marines is one of the greatest honors we have as officers,” Copeland said. "Families entrust their sons and daughters to the Marine Corps, and us by extension. With that comes the responsibility to care for them, develop them and set them up for success. We couldn’t accomplish our mission without the families who support them.”

The Marines’ response demonstrated how disciplined training, resilient minds, and trust among teammates has cultivated a legacy of honor. Whether safeguarding the “Oldest Post of the Corps,” or preparing to return to the Fleet Marine Force, 8th & I Marines remain steadfast in how they represent the Marine Corps when the Nation calls.

items.title: Navy Expeditionary Medicine training center changes command, accelerating ready medical force
items.author: Arsenio R. Cortez Jr.
items.summary: Capt. George Brand relieved Capt. Kevin Bailey as commanding officer of the Naval Expeditionary Medicine Warfighter Development Center during a change of command ceremony held aboard Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton on Sept. 3, 2026.
items.body:
CAMP PENDLETON, Calif. — Capt. George Brand relieved Capt. Kevin Bailey as commanding officer of the Naval Expeditionary Medicine Warfighter Development Center during a change of command ceremony held aboard Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton on Sept. 3, 2026. Rear Adm. Kevin Brown, commander of Naval Medical Forces Pacific, presided over the ceremony, commending the NEMWDC for rapidly evolving into the cornerstone of operational readiness for Navy Medicine, bridging the gap between traditional military treatment facilities and the rigorous medical requirements of the modern warfighter operating in distributed and contested theaters. Brown traced the historical lineage of the command from the initial groundbreaking of the Fleet Hospital Training Activity in 1986 through the Naval Expeditionary Medical Training Institute, culminating in the establishment of NEMWDC as an Echelon 4 command in October 2024. He emphasized that this transformation operationalized medical training to directly match the demands of future conflict, ensuring deployed teams possess the capabilities needed to save lives on the battlefield and project naval power worldwide. "This is where we prepare Expeditionary Medicine teams to save lives, projecting Navy Medicine power that deters aggression and supports combat operations," Brown said. "Today is more than a change of command. It's a chance to reflect on the strategic importance of Navy Medicine in defending our nation, sustaining our warfighters, and strengthening alliances. And none of that is possible without the exemplary leadership Capt. Bailey has demonstrated during his tour." Highlighting Bailey’s 23-month tenure, Brown detailed the command's operational achievements, which included leading Operational Readiness Evaluations for more than 1,800 medical and non-medical personnel and certifying more than 1,100 expeditionary medical personnel across the joint force. Under Bailey’s watch, the command rigorously validated 38 En Route Care Systems, 19 Expeditionary Resuscitative Surgical Systems, five Expeditionary Medical Facilities, and four forward-deployable Preventive Medicine units, while maintaining complete accountability of critical platforms and passing a comprehensive Medical Inspector General inspection within seven weeks of establishment. Brown also underscored Bailey's focus on joint integration, noting that exercises routinely incorporated U.S. Air Force aeromedical evacuation teams, Army veterinary units, and Navy Seabees to cultivate cohesive joint patient movement and tactical survivability. As Bailey transitions to his next assignment at the Bureau of Medicine and Surgery in Falls Church, Virginia, Brown noted that his operational focus left an enduring mark on the readiness of the Navy Medicine enterprise. Addressing the NEMWDC staff, Bailey reflected on the collective effort of the Sailors and civilian professionals who built the command's capabilities from the deckplate up. He highlighted how student feedback directly reshaped curriculum development, transitioning classroom theory into high-stress, reality-tested training that incorporated advanced trauma moulage, high-fidelity manikins, and complex command-and-control scenarios in austere environments. "Two short years ago, few on the deckplates even knew what an 'EXMED' was," Bailey said. "Today, NEMWDC sets the standard across the enterprise. To the Sailors and staff of NEMWDC, you built this command brick by brick. NEMWDC’s transition wasn’t an overnight overhaul. It was hundreds of small wins earned by dedicated professionals. " Brand, a Nurse Corps officer who previously served as the director of education and training at NMFP, arrives with extensive operational experience across the Marine Corps, surface fleet, and aviation communities. Returning to the grounds where he trained as an ensign, returned as a lieutenant, and later served as assistant officer-in-charge preparing medical teams for deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan, Brand reaffirmed his commitment to operational excellence and warfighter survivability. "NEMWDC is a premier command with a critical, no-fail mission," Brand said. "If our military treatment facilities are the foundry of Navy Medicine, NEMWDC is the forge, the place where we transform medical capability into ready expeditionary medical forces required for the distributed maritime environment." Brand closed by expressing gratitude to his family and pledging to lead focusing on personnel proficiencies as NEMWDC continues to forge the future of Expeditionary Medicine. “The true engine of this command is our deckplate leadership and personnel,” Brand said. “Rain or shine, you work relentlessly to turn individual health care providers into cohesive, ready expeditionary units. I am deeply honored to take the helm and lead this incredible team.” NEMWDC, located at Camp Pendleton, serves as Navy Medicine’s center of excellence for Expeditionary Medicine training. The command develops, delivers, and sustains advanced, scenario-based training to ensure medical personnel are ready to support combat operations across the globe. NEMWDC’s programs strengthen warfighter readiness and prepare Sailors to provide critical care anytime, anywhere.

items.title: Lost in 1941, WWII Soldier Will Be Laid to Rest at Omaha National Cemetery
items.author: Daniela Vestal
items.summary: The remains of U.S. Army Air Forces Sgt. Robert C. Pierce, 28, who was captured and died as a prisoner of war during World War II, will be interred Sept. 8 at Omaha national Cemetery in Omaha, Nebraska. Services and interment are being coordinated by Braman Mortuary, 402-895-3400.
items.body:
FORT KNOX, Ky. – The remains of U.S. Army Air Forces Sgt. Robert C. Pierce, 28, who was captured and died as a prisoner of war during World War II, will be interred Sept. 8 at Omaha national Cemetery in Omaha, Nebraska. Services and interment are being coordinated by Braman Mortuary, 402-895-3400. In late 1941, Pierce was a member of the 7th Materiel Squadron, 5th Air Base Group, when Japanese forces invaded the Philippine Islands in December. Intense fighting continued until the surrender of the Bataan peninsula on April 9, 1942, and of Corregidor Island on May 6, 1942. Thousands of U.S. and Filipino service members were captured and interned at POW camps. Pierce was among those reported captured when U.S. forces in Bataan surrendered to the Japanese. They were subjected to the 65-mile Bataan Death March and then held at the Cabanatuan POW camp. More than 2,500 POWs perished in this camp during the war. According to prison camp and other historical records, Pierce died Nov. 22, 1942, and was buried along with other deceased prisoners in the local Cabanatuan Camp Cemetery in Common Grave 807. The Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency accounted for Pierce on Jan. 6, 2026. For more information on DPAA’s efforts to locate and identify Pierce, please visit: https://www.dpaa.mil/News-Stories/ID-Announcements/Article/4442925/airman-accounted-for-from-world-war-ii-pierce-r/ U.S. Army Human Resources Command’s Past Conflict Repatriations Branch plays a vital role in the process of identifying, locating and contacting subsequent generation family members of Soldiers missing or killed in action during WWII and the Korean War to positively identify previously undiscovered or unknown remains. Media interested in covering and/or obtaining more information about the funeral and interment should contact Braman Mortuary, 402-895-3400.

items.title: U.S. Coast Guard participates in Combined Joint Logistics Over-the-Shore training exercise with the Republic of Korea

CAMP HUMPHREYS, South Korea — U.S. Coast Guard Port Security Unit (PSU) 309 crew members recently returned to Port Clinton, Ohio, after demonstrating waterside security capabilities during U.S. Transportation Command’s Combined Joint Logistics Over-the-Shore (CJLOTS) exercise held July 10–20 in Pohang.

The Pacific is home to five of the seven U.S. security alliances: Australia, Japan, the Philippines, Thailand, and the Republic of Korea (ROK). This was the first time in nine years that the ROK and the United States conducted this complex, combined training event.

The international logistics exercise tests the ability of U.S. forces to mobilize and transport personnel and materiel, and establish logistics lines in a simulated contested environment.

More than 1,900 service members from the U.S. Army, U.S. Marine Corps, U.S. Navy, ROK Navy, and ROK Coast Guard participated in the exercise.

The training focused on the process of discharging military cargo from ships at sea to an undeveloped shoreline. ROK and U.S. service members worked together to establish temporary port facilities to deliver equipment, vehicles and supplies, ensuring combined forces can sustain operations in any environment or degraded port scenario.

“During CJLOTS 26, PSU 309 exemplified the U.S. Coast Guard’s hallmark agility and operational flexibility, proving our ability to seamlessly integrate into the joint and combined command structure and demonstrate our outstanding value to the Joint Force and steadfast commitment to the U.S. Pacific Command area of responsibility,” said Cmdr. Kristopher Nolan, PSU 309’s commanding officer.

PSU 309’s participation highlighted the Coast Guard’s adaptability within a combatant command, providing waterside security to U.S. and ROK forces in a 24-hour operational environment and deterring 70 recreational vessels from entering the security zone.

Conducted in the spirit of the Oct. 1, 1953, ROK–U.S. Mutual Defense Treaty, CJLOTS 26 reinforces the alliance’s role as the linchpin of regional peace and security and reaffirms the United States’ unwavering commitment to the defense of the Republic of Korea.

PSU missions include providing waterborne and land-based protection for shipping and critical port facilities. PSU 309 is one of eight units capable of global deployment within 96 hours of recall. PSUs also support domestic missions, including humanitarian assistance, and can operate independently or alongside other Department of War units.

items.title: Lost in 1945, WWII Flyer Will Be Laid to Rest in Maryland
items.author: Daniela Vestal
items.summary: The remains of U.S. Army Air Forces 1st Lt. Walter R. Bateman, who was listed as missing in action during World War II, will be interred Sept. 6 at Union Chapel United Methodist Church Cemetery in Joppatowne, Maryland. Services and interment are being coordinated by Schimunek Funeral Home.
items.body:
FORT KNOX, Ky. – The remains of U.S. Army Air Forces 1st Lt. Walter R. Bateman, who was listed as missing in action during World War II, will be interred Sept. 6 at Union Chapel United Methodist Church Cemetery in Joppatowne, Maryland. Services and interment are being coordinated by Schimunek Funeral Home. Bateman entered the service from Maryland and served in the 67th Bombardment Squadron, 44th Bombardment Group. On Aug. 16, 1943, he piloted a B-24D Liberator that took off from Benina, Libya, along with 25 other B-24s on a bombing mission against enemy airfields at Foggia, Italy. The operation inflicted heavy damage on the targets, but seven of the aircraft, including this B-24D, failed to return to base. Searchers found no possible crash location nor any signs or remains of the 10 missing crew members. In April 1945, the American Graves Registration Command recovered several unidentified, commingled sets of remains buried in the Cemetery of Lacedonia, Italy. The remains were reportedly of American airmen who were shot down on Aug. 16, 1943. Investigators located the aircraft wreckage but could not find any information to identify the aircraft at the crash site. The remains could not be identified at the time and were interred as unknowns in the U.S. Military Cemetery in Naples. In June 2022, the Department of Defense and American Battle Monuments Commission exhumed the unknowns and transferred them to the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency laboratory. There, scientists used modern forensic techniques to identify Bateman. The Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency accounted for Bateman on May 29, 2026. For more information on DPAA’s efforts to locate and identify Bateman, please visit: https://dpaa-mil.sites.crmforce.mil/dpaaProfile?id=a0Jt0000000Xdf2EAC U.S. Army Human Resources Command’s Past Conflict Repatriations Branch plays a vital role in the process of identifying, locating and contacting subsequent generation family members of Soldiers missing or killed in action during WWII and the Korean War to positively identify previously undiscovered or unknown remains. Media interested in covering and/or obtaining more information about the funeral and interment should contact Schimunek Funeral Home, 410-638-5360.

items.title: US Air Force speeds Reaper successor timeline after Iran losses
items.author: Michael Scanlon
items.summary: The Air Force is accelerating its timeline for a cheaper, more expendable successor to the MQ-9A Reaper after combat losses.
items.body:
MilTech

US Air Force speeds Reaper successor timeline after Iran losses

An MQ-9 Reaper, armed with GBU-12 Paveway II laser guided munitions and AGM-114 Hellfire missiles, flies a combat mission over southern Afghanistan. (Lt. Col. Leslie Pratt/U.S. Air Force)

The U.S. Air Force is accelerating its timeline for a cheaper, more expendable successor to the MQ-9A Reaper, officials said Sept. 3, after combat losses left the service unwilling to wait out the rest of the drone’s life.

Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s chief modernization officer, told reporters at the Pentagon that a follow-on was already under discussion as the MQ-9 aged out.

“Although we have plenty of MQ-9As today, we are going through them at a rate that is concerning to us,” he said, according to Breaking Defense , which covered the briefing.

Defense Daily reported that Air Force Secretary Troy Meink directed the acceleration, and that the fiscal 2031 target of 20 mission-ready aircraft could be pulled forward by about two years.

In May, Lt. Gen. David Tabor told the Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Airland the fleet was down to about 135 aircraft , roughly 54 below the service’s 189-aircraft floor. Niemi did not update the inventory.

Backfilling the fleet is difficult. General Atomics shut down MQ-9A production in 2025, and Tabor said the service was pursuing a short-term buy of existing MQ-9A airframes in fiscal 2026. Niemi said Sept. 3 that budget constraints make buying a large number of upgraded MQ-9B SkyGuardians unrealistic. It is a misconception, he said, that the Air Force could write a check and take delivery of 100 aircraft.

A Congressional Research Service Insight updated May 13 cited an April 9 news report of 24 Reapers lost since military operations against Iran began in February, and said it was unclear whether the Pentagon had given Congress an accounting. The Washington Post reported Aug. 13 , citing three U.S. officials, that at least 45 had been lost, roughly 25% of the fleet.

Niemi signed requirements in May for a cheaper, modular, mass-producible aircraft.

That program, Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMA, opened as a Defense Innovation Unit competition July 7 with the Air Force as partner. The solicitation, which closed July 23, asked for a drone that could fly Reaper-class strike, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, electronic warfare and communications-relay missions cheaply enough to absorb losses. It called for at least 2,800 pounds of payload and an 8,000-nautical-mile one-way ferry range.

That is the aircraft Niemi now prices against Collaborative Combat Aircraft, or CCA. He put CCA air vehicles near $20 million and MMA at about half that, Defense Daily reported.

An Air Force spokesperson said those figures are for the air vehicle only, not a fully missionized aircraft, according to Breaking Defense . In May, Niemi told senators a Reaper with a full sensor package can cost up to $50 million. At the Sept. 3 briefing, he said the Air Force will probably field at least 180 MMA drones.

Niemi argued the Reaper’s value is not the airframe.

“What makes the MQ-9 special has nothing to do with the aircraft itself,” he said, calling its speed, altitude and range decades-old technology.

Initial MMA versions, he said, will rely on proven technology rather than new systems to hit the price. He described a long-aspect-wing turboprop in the “4,000 miles-type class,” farther and heavier than a CCA but slower. Officials did not say how that class relates to the 8,000-nautical-mile ferry range in the July notice.

General Atomics is bidding a design it calls Wildfire, first reported by Aviation Week in August. Spokesman C. Mark Brinkley told Air & Space Forces Magazine it “meets every wish on the [MMA] list and exceeds most of them,” but declined to give capabilities or cost. The company has not released images.

Brinkley told The War Zone in August that treating MMA as a Reaper replacement misses the immediate need for a backfill. Wildfire does not depend on winning the competition, he said, and “we can deliver Wildfires years earlier than the current schedule.”

He framed the design targets as considerations rather than specs, among them a 10,000-nautical-mile ferry range, four Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles and 100 aircraft under semi-autonomous control.

Col. Todd Dye, senior materiel leader in the Air Force’s medium-altitude intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance division, said awards for MMA concept refinement were expected in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, Breaking Defense reported .

Officials did not announce a new date at the Sept. 3 briefing.

Michael Scanlon is a defense journalist covering air and space warfare. A former U.S. Air Force A-10 crew chief, he has supported land and sea programs for the U.S. Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard.

items.title: Lost in 1950, Korean War Soldier Returns to Rest in Illinois
items.author: Daniela Vestal
items.summary: FORT KNOX, Ky. – The remains of U.S. Army Pfc. Andrew E. Hathaway, 18, killed during the Korean War, will be interred Sept. 5 at New Milford Cemetery in Rockford, Illinois. Service and interment are being coordinated by Honquest Family Funeral Home.
items.body:
FORT KNOX, Ky. – The remains of U.S. Army Pfc. Andrew E. Hathaway, 18,killed during the Korean War,will be interred Sept. 5 at New Milford Cemetery in Rockford, Illinois. Service and interment are being coordinated by Honquest Family Funeral Home. In late 1950, Hathaway was a member of Company K, 3rd Battalion, 35th Infantry Regiment, 25th Infantry Division. He was reportedly killed on Nov. 28, after the Battle of the Ch’ongch’on River, Republic of Korea. Returning POWs reported that Hathaway was held at Camp 5 in Pyoktong, North Korea, where he died on an unknown date. The Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency accounted for Hathaway on April 3, 2025. items.title: Army-made motors power historic ‘Game of Drones’ flight
items.author: Jason Kaneshiro
items.summary: The Army Materiel Command’s motors powered a first of its kind flight.
items.body:
EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE, Calif.–A historic unmanned aerial system flight broke the endurance record for an independently battery-powered software designed 3D-printed group 1 drone using the power of Army-manufactured motors during Defense Contract Management Agency’s “Game of Drones” event here July 16.

The Army is not known for manufacturing components, but in a first of its kind demonstration, the Army Materiel Command’s drone motors proved its capabilities by setting a new endurance world record of 521 minutes and 43 seconds.

Army Capt. Lee Washburn, AMC military liaison for advanced manufacturing of small UAS, said the motors were one of the very first to come off the production line at the Tobyhanna Army Depot, Pennsylvania.

“AMC manufactured two 3115 sized brushless disc current (BLDC) motors to take part in ‘Game of Drones,’” Washburn said. “This capability to produce BLDC motors domestically, and within the Army’s Organic Industrial Base, is brand new as the ribbon cutting of the facility was only held on June 30, 2026 .”

AMC’s goal is to manufacture sUAS components utilizing a clean supply chain that is decoupled from foreign dependencies and have components on DCMA’s https://bluelist.appsplatformportals.us/ that are available for the U.S. military and industry to procure.

Jon Strzelec, AMC advanced manufacturing lead for sUAS, said when the president signed the https://safe.menlosecurity.com/doc/docview/viewer/docN15B3010D6692bbc391ae804943b602ee2eb938489830a0140197c50ff861bbe1d089f0bd962f, Army Lt. Gen. Chris Mohan, AMC commanding general, looked to the Organic Industrial Base of 23 depots, arsenals and ammunition plants that are government-owned, to support the resident’s intent.

“AMC received funding invest in the OIB in an effort to bring manufacturing of critical sUAS components back into the United States,” Strzelec said. “Brushless direct current motors are just one of the components that AMC is leveraging the OIB to produce.”

AMC also produces drone frames at Rock Island Arsenal-Joint Manufacturing and Technology Center, Illinois; batteries at Red River Army Depot, Texas; and circuit cards along with the BLDC motors at Tobyhanna Army Depot.

“‘Game of Drones’ was proof that industry and the government can work together in creative ways to create exceptional results,” Strzelec said. “The event showcases exactly what the Army set out to do – provide opportunities for industry to partner with the Army and let the Army leverage the innovation and technical depth of industry. The event is proof that with collaboration between industry and the Army, we can achieve record-breaking results.”

AMC’s goal is to continue to participate in events that demonstrate their capabilities and help refine components for the warfighter based upon realistic testing.

Washburn said providing clean supply chain solutions in support of Drone Dominance is another critical goal. “AMC is proud to provide materiel solutions to support innovation across the uncrewed systems spectrum,” Washburn said. “As AMC’s production efforts across the OIB continues to expand into UAS chassis and bodies, battery solutions, circuit card assemblies, and injection molding of parts such as propellors, we will continue to work with DCMA in not only blue listing these components but also providing them to the Air Force Experimental Test Force for ‘Game of Drones’ events to innovate and break other performance and endurance records in support of Drone Dominance and our nation’s defense.”

The https://bluelist.appsplatformportals.us/ is an aggregated list of compliant unmanned systems and components for the Department of War. The Blue List was transferred to DCMA from the Defense Innovation Unit in 2025 and takes a holistic approach to continuously and rapidly vet commercial UAS technology for DOW.

The Blue List creates confidence in trusted components before they become part of larger systems, said Air Force Col. Dustin Thomas, DCMA Unmanned Systems Experimental commander.

“We must ensure that our wartime supply chains remain available. We cannot become dependent upon adversary-controlled manufacturing,” Thomas said. “To that end, we need components from trusted sources that will continue to exist during conflict.”

If an adversary can simply stop producing a critical component, that component was never truly trustworthy. The goal of the Blue List is to establish trust at the component level instead of repeatedly rebuilding and validating trust for every new platform.

“When it began, the Blue List was primarily focused on blue listing platforms, and later it began to blue list specific components. When DCMA took over the Blue List, we made a big push to shift to components,” Thomas said. “The reason to focus on components is that we can reduce our effort, manpower, and workload on drones that already have components that have gone through the Blue List process.”

This change in focus helps to ensure that we can continue fighting past day one, Thomas said.

items.title: Blue List makes waves in the Pacific
items.author: Jason Kaneshiro
items.summary: DCMA’s Blue List team engaged with units in Hawaii to see emerging capabilities on the islands.
items.body:
HONOLULU–Members of Defense Contract Management Agency’s [Blue List](https://tyrionprod.servicenowservices.com/gsp?id=gsp_index) team visited units in Hawaii during the biennial Rim of the Pacific exercise to see emerging capabilities on the islands July 7-9. The group engaged Army, Navy and Marine Corps stakeholders working on developing unmanned systems and additive manufacturing technologies. “We'd been extremely busy and getting pulled left and right and talking with people, and so it's been a really good visit from that standpoint to understand how they're thinking and what their needs are,” said Army Maj. Eric Scholl, Blue List program integrator. During the engagement, agency experts visited the 25th Infantry Division’s [“Lightning Lab”](https://www.army.mil/article/292503/lanpac_2026_soldier_driven_solutions_showcased_by_lightning_labs) at Schofield Barracks. “They are building their own drones for units here,” Scholl said. “We got to tour their facility where they produce and have their printers and where they build their drones.” The Blue List team then moved to one of the ranges on base where the Naval Information Warfare Center was training one of their targeting algorithms to identify UAS, and then to a range across the island where they were training a counter-UAS platform to identify drones coming off of the water onto the land. The team also toured [The Forge](https://www.army.mil/article/287567/usindopacom_commander_attends_soft_opening_of_the_forge_an_advanced_manufacturing_facility_in_hawaii), an advanced manufacturing facility that uses 3D printing, precision casting, forging, and rapid prototyping for the Navy and joint forces. “It's where they're standing up production on the islands to be able to produce for the fleet as they need items,” Scholl said. “They're developing a hub and spoke model, so the hub would be here on the main island.” They also toured their foundry, where they smelted metal in a mobilized container that they had repurposed, before moving to the [Joint Advanced Manufacturing Cell](https://nps.edu/-/largest-advanced-manufacturing-demonstration-in-department-of-war-history-set-for-rimpac-2026) hosted by the Naval Postgraduate School. The JAMC produced replacement parts and supported distributed logistics. “We were watching in real time as they were processing production requests,” Scholl said. “It wasn’t just drones, but it's really any piece or part that the fleet might need, both in plastics and in metal.” Scholl said they briefed them on the Blue List, how DCMA would be able to connect with them and their efforts. The [Blue List](https://tyrionprod.servicenowservices.com/gsp?id=gsp_index) is an aggregated list of compliant unmanned systems and components approved for purchase and operation by the War Department. Air Force Col. Dustin Thomas, DCMA Unmanned Systems-Experimental commander, said the anecdote from range control highlights how the Blue List can serve as a compliance standard. “If we don't have these compliance standards set, then everyone's going to use slightly different rules,” Thomas said. “Trust in platforms and components becomes something that continuously grows rather than something established once during certification.” The Blue List’s shift in focus from risk management to include compliance with standards is intended to support unit commander’s desires to rapidly get trusted equipment into the hands of their end users. “The standards that we're building are there for a reason,” Thomas said. “They're there so that we can continue fighting after day one.” The Blue List was transferred to DCMA from the [Defense Innovation Unit](https://www.diu.mil/) in 2025 and takes a holistic approach to continuously and rapidly vet commercial UAS technology for DOW.

items.title: My DCMA Remember 9/11: David Fagan
items.author: Elizabeth Szoke
items.summary: David Fagan shares how the events of Sept. 11, 2001, shaped his life.
items.body:
FORT LEE, Va.–My DCMA “Remember 9/11” editionshowcasesthe Defense Contract Management Agency’s experienced and dedicated workforce as they reflect on the events of Sept. 11, 2001. The campaign highlights that tragic day’s personal and professional impact on agency team members. Today, David Fagan shares his story.

My name is David Fagan, and this is “My DCMA.”

On Sept. 11, 2001, I was an intern working at thethen Defense Contract Management Command’sNorthrop Grumman Baltimore office. I remember walking across the parking lot after listening to the radio during my drive to work. Everything had seemed normal.

In the few minutes it took me to leave my car and enter the building, everything changed.When I walked in, everyone was gathered around a television in the break room. The first plane had already struck the World Trade Center. As a New Yorker, I was concerned, but I did not yet understand themagnitudeof what had happened. We did not know the size of theaircraft, and I assumed it had been a terrible accident.

When the second plane struck, we realized it was intentional and our nation was under attack. For my generation of New Yorkers, thetwintowers defined the city’s skyline. Watching both towers fall felt unreal, like something from science fiction; artificial intelligence before AI.Then the Pentagon was attacked. The place where I had grown up and the region where I was living were both struck on the same day.

Earlier in 2001, I had questioned my place in government service. I had completed extensive training in software acquisition, software development lifecyclesand systems development, but I did not fully understand how it connected to a larger purpose.

After 9/11, activity at the Northrop Grumman facility increased dramatically as the nation prepared for operations in Afghanistan. The plant supported radar, sensors and other systems needed by the warfighter. Suddenly, all the training that had once seemed abstract made sense.

I understood that my job was to help ensure those systems worked properly, were delivered on time and were provided at the right price. The people deploying in defense of our country needed equipment they could depend on.Almost overnight, I went from wondering whether I wanted to remain in government to knowing I had a job to do.

I have never served in the military, as so many people at DCMA have. Everyone’s connection to the agency’s mission is different. Those who put on the uniform and raised their right hand have a connection I would never claim to share.

Service members train for war. For civilians like me, 9/11 was what war looked like when it reached home. That experience gave me my own connection to DCMA’s mission and the people who serve. It showed me why our work matters and why caring for those who wear the uniform is a responsibility shared by the entire defense community.

My path to the agency began after I earned a master’s degree in education from the University of Tennessee. I visited my brother, who was serving in the Navy and working for a predecessor organization of DCMA at Fort Belvoir, Virginia. He introduced me to his supervisor, and that meeting eventually led to an offer to join the intern program. I entered government service in May 1998 and have been part of the mission ever since.

Today, I serve as a lead software policy analyst with DCMA’s Technical Directorate. I write and manage policy supporting approximately 260 software acquisition professionals in the field. They help ensure contractors developing software meet the terms of their contracts and deliver products that work properly at theappropriate price.

I also advocate for the workforce’s needs at headquarters, answer policy questions and connect DCMA’s field software community with agency leadership. As technology evolves, we are exploring how artificial intelligence can help field personnel perform their jobs more efficiently, particularly when staffing and resources are limited. After 28 years, I know I am closer to the end of my career than the beginning. That makes passing along knowledge increasingly important to me.

There will come a day when no oneremainingat DCMA will have served in one of its predecessor organizations. Eventually, no one in the agency will have personally experienced 9/11 as a member of the workforce. We must pass down more than technical knowledge. We must also share our stories, our sense of urgency and our culture.

DCMA is not a large organization, but it has an exceptionally important mission. Artificial intelligence can help usretainand use information, but technology alone cannot preserve an organization’s soul. Wehave toshare the experiences that explain why the work matters and pass our commitment and esprit de corps from one generation to the next.

The country came together after 9/11, but that unity followed tremendous pain. We should also remember that some Muslim and Middle Eastern Americans were treated unfairly in the aftermath. Remembering 9/11 means learning from the entire experience and embracing our fellow citizens as Americans.

The effects of that day continue to move through our workforce like ripples across a pond. Someone may believe they have no personal connection to 9/11, but I would encourage them to listen to their colleagues’ stories. Its impactremainspresent in our agency and our mission 25 years later.

I would never wish the experience of that day on anyone. As we move farther away from it, however, I do not want us to lose the urgency it brought to our work.

“Never forget” is more than a saying. We must never forget how we felt that day, why our mission matters and what we are here to protect.

Editor’s note:DCMA’s “Remember 9/11” is a campaign reflecting on the events of Sept. 11, 2001,and thelasting impact 25 years later through stories of remembrance,resilienceand service. We invite you to share your story by emailingtheDCMA Public Affairs inbox. DCMA Public Affairs hopes to share as many stories as possible but cannot guarantee every submission will be published.

items.title: Air Force Speeding Up New Low-Cost Drone Program after Heavy MQ-9 Losses Against Iran
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: The Air Force is accelerating its plans to field an MQ-9A replacement in the wake of heavy Reaper losses in operations against Iran, top officials said Sept. 3, and they’re targeting a price point of just $10 million per aircraft. The post Air Force Speeding Up New Low-Cost Drone Program after Heavy MQ-9 Losses Against Iran appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Air Force Speeding Up New Low-Cost Drone Program after Heavy MQ-9 Losses Against Iran

Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Air Force is accelerating its plans to field an MQ-9A replacement in the wake of heavy Reaper losses in operations against Iran, top officials said Sept. 3, and they’re targeting a price point of just $10 million per aircraft.

Back in July, the Air Force and the Defense Innovation Unit announced plans to develop a low-cost drone to do all the missions that an MQ-9 can do today, and when necessary fly in groups to overwhelm an enemy’s anti-drone capabilities and force them to expend large numbers of munitions. They called the effort Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMA .

At the time, officials said they wanted to have a prototype to test fly within 21 months of a contract, and then 20 mission-ready aircraft by fiscal 2031 to achieve initial operating capability.

Now, though, officials are targeting a more ambitious timeline. During a media roundtable at the Pentagon, DIU military deputy Maj. Gen. Joseph Kunkel said the MMA program will try to follow DIU’s typical timeframe of prototyping a system within a year of a contract, and then fielding it at scale within three years—as soon as 2029.

Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s new chief modernization officer, said those goals changed “fairly recently,” when Air Force Secretary Troy Meink “called us in and said ‘You need to move faster.’”

That urgency, Niemi acknowledged, came at least partly in response to the significant losses the MQ-9 fleet has taken in the past year or so during operations against Iran and Iranian-backed militias. Since the start of the Iran war, the Air Force has lost at least 45 MQ-9s, roughly a quarter of its fleet. The service was already thinking about what it needed to succeed the MQ-9 as a medium-altitude intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance platform, but Niemi said the combat losses pushed it to move faster.

“Although we have plenty of MQ-9As today, we are going through them at a rate that is concerning to us,” Niemi said.

Replacing, Not Reinventing, the MQ-9

The MQ-9 has long been a workhorse of the Air Force fleet, valued by combatant commanders for its long endurance, loitering ability, and ability to combine strike and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach called the Reaper the “most valuable player” of Operation Epic Fury in a May congressional hearing.

Unsurprisingly, then, officials said they were eager to replace the ones lost in combat. Niemi said the Air Force has “spent a lot of time and energy” in recent months trying to figure out how to do so and found “there’s not a lot of good options to immediately replace those aircraft.”

The Air Force considered General Atomics’ MQ-9B, a larger and more complex—and more expensive—version of the MQ-9A, Niemi said. Ultimately, officials concluded the MQ-9B was not the right choice because the Air Force needed something more “attritable,” or inexpensive enough to be fielded in large numbers and easily replaced if lost in combat.

“If you don’t like losing an MQ-9A that cost on the order of $50 million, with the sensors, you’re probably not going to like losing an MQ-9B at a higher price point,” Niemi said.

For that reason, the Air Force decided to go all-in on the MMA concept. The Air Force plans to field at least 180 of the drones, Niemi said, but probably more than that.

In order to move fast and keep costs down, Niemi said the Air Force plans to “accept prudent risk” on the MMA program. Kunkel also said the Air Force wants “significantly increased levels of competition” to keep costs down.

As the Air Force wrote out what attributes MMA drones would need, Niemi added, it tried to allow as much flexibility as possible and not include hyper-specific requirements that “push technology to the very edge.”

“When that happens, you’re going to pay a lot for it, because it’s hard to do,” Niemi said. “It takes a lot of engineering, cutting-edge science, emergent technologies, things like that. So we’re trying to be more aligned with sort of an ‘80 percent is good enough,’ [using] mature technologies” approach.

That means MMA won’t have the latest and greatest flight control systems, engines, or manufacturing processes, he said—and they’ll actually resemble the MQ-9 in some key ways: they’ll likely have long-aspect wings and will likely be powered by turboprop engines.

One way officials are looking to differ from the MQ-9, though, are higher levels of autonomy and automation than the MQ-9A has today, Niemi said—“more mouse clicks and keyboard strokes instead of a stick and throttle.” That will reduce the number of Airmen needed to operate MMA drones and allow a single Airman to operate multiple drones simultaneously.

At the same time, Niemi said MMAs won’t have the same level of autonomy as the Air Force’s flagship autonomous drone program, Collaborative Combat Aircraft.

“It’s not going out and autonomously finding targets and employing weapons,” Niemi said of the MMA drone. “It’s more like a truck that’s carrying packages, whether it’s a sensor package or whether it’s a weapon, to a point where it can be employed.”

CCAs and MMAs

While CCAs and MMAs will both be unmanned and have some kind of autonomy software, Niemi was quick to note there will be major differences between the two.

“They’re going to look very different,” Niemi said. The MMA is “going to look like an MQ-9, and [CCA is] going to look more like a fighter, like you’ve seen in the current too CCAs that we’re flying.”

The Air Force wants MMA drones to be able to fly about 4,000 miles—more than twice the expected range of autonomous Collaborative Combat Aircraft drones—and carry a heavy payload, although they will be slower than CCAs, Niemi said.

Those differences extend to price, too—while the Air Force is targeting $10 million for an MMA drone, it’s hoping for $20 million per CCA once they reach full production. Those costs are for just the base aircraft, excluding sensors, weapons or other equipment that might be loaded onto them.

From an acquisition perspective, the Air Force is hoping to use the same methods across the CCA and MMA programs to keep costs down and production simple.

That includes moving quickly to award contracts and keeping several vendors on contract to provide a variety of drones. Like CCAs, MMA drones will also use open architecture , Niemi said. That will ensure the drones have standardized interfaces and could be easily upgraded with newer sensor packages or weapons capabilities, even from different vendors, he said. This would also allow MMAs to be tailored with the gear needed for a particular mission.

“If you want to build a package that’s going to go on this new aircraft, as long as it conforms to this [standardized interface], we can do it very speedily and very readily,” Niemi said. “That’s something we struggle with at the opposite end of the spectrum, something like the F-35, where it’s very very hard to incorporate new things onto it, because of the construct and the architecture of that system.”

The Air Force also wants manufacturers to be able to produce MMA drones in large numbers, Niemi said, but also be able to ramp production up or down as needed, such as if the Air Force started losing large numbers in a heated conflict. Keeping MMAs simple is the best way to ensure that production flexibility, he said.

“If you wanted to suddenly ramp up production of something like an F-35, it’s not a limiting factor so much as money, as the ability to build out your production capacity and actually crank more of those things out,” Niemi said. “And the more complex the aircraft, the harder that problem is. … In major combat operations, depending on who you’re fighting, we could be losing dozens [of MMA drones] a day, and so you have to figure out how do you adjust the industrial capacity in order to make [necessary production levels] happen.”

General Atomics, which also makes the MQ-9, is planning to pitch a newly designed drone it calls Wildfire for the MMA program.

“Our new Wildfire aircraft addresses all of the concerns posed by the MMA solicitation,” General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a statement to reporters. “We can deliver years earlier and maintain the same high quality. You can have everything that makes Reaper special, plus more, at a price that doesn’t break the bank.”

items.title: Fresh US Fighter Jets Rotate into Middle East as Trump Tries to Up Pressure on Iran
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: The U.S. is rotating fresh fighter squadrons to the Middle East to support the Trump administration’s open-ended campaign of economic and military pressure against Iran. The post Fresh US Fighter Jets Rotate into Middle East as Trump Tries to Up Pressure on Iran appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Fresh US Fighter Jets Rotate into Middle East as Trump Tries to Up Pressure on Iran

Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The U.S. is rotating fresh fighter squadrons to the Middle East to support the Trump administration’s open-ended pressure campaign against Iran.

The move will free up units that have been based in the region far beyond the Air Force’s usual six-month deployments. More fighter unit rotations are expected in the coming weeks.

Units on their way home include the 158th Fighter Wing of the Vermont Air National Guard, which flies F-35 Lightning II aircraft. F-16 Fighting Falcon s from the 555th Fighter Squadron based at Aviano Air Base, Italy, are also returning, according to people familiar with the matter and data collected by the open-source group the Military Air Tracking Alliance .

The departing units have been deployed overseas since last year. The Vermont F-35s first deployed to Puerto Rico in December 2025 and supported the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January, before deploying to the Middle East ahead of the U.S. air war against Iran. The Vermont ANG’s F-35s were spotted transiting through RAF Lakenheath, U.K., on their way back home. The F-16s from the 555th Fighter Squadron had been deployed to the Middle East since November.

Arriving in CENTCOM are F-16s from the Ohio Air National Guard’s 180th Fighter Wing. Twelve F-16s from the Ohio ANG departed Lajes in the Azores on Sept. 4, according to local aircraft spotters. The planes, which arrived on the Portuguese island on Aug. 29, are due to head to the Middle East.

A spokesman for U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last month that the U.S. is stepping up its economic sanctions campaign to try to stop Iran from interfering with oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz while pressing Tehran to make concessions on its nuclear program. That is in addition to the ongoing American maritime blockade.

“If we are doing the maximum economic pressure, then that means that likely there will not be a large-scale kinetic restart,” Bessent told CNBC last month.

But U.S. officials also say that the increased economic pressure might lead Iran to retaliate militarily. Fighting in the region flared up late last month when the U.S. struck Iranian launchers that were preparing to launch rockets with mines into the strait, and Iran retaliated by firing ballistic missiles at American forces in Jordan.

The new U.S. pressure campaign is likely to reduce the need for defensive and offensive munitions in the near term. But it still requires an ongoing military presence in the region and efforts to manage operational demands on the force.

The USS Abraham Lincoln docked in Thailand earlier this week after spending nine months at sea. The Lincoln took part in Operation Epic Fury—which officially lasted from Feb. 28 to early April—and then helped enforce a U.S. military blockade of Iranian ports and partook in tit-for-tat clashes against the Iranians for months.

items.title: Trump to travel aboard Qatari-donated Air Force One to Ireland
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump will use the Qatari-donated jet to travel to Ireland next week, the plane's first international trip since the swap in Turkey.
items.body:
Daily News Roundup

Trump to travel aboard Qatari-donated Air Force One to Ireland

U.S. President Donald Trump arrives aboard the new Qatari-gifted Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, U.S., July 9, 2026. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

U.S. President Donald Trump plans to fly to Ireland next week aboard the Boeing 747 Qatari-donated jet for the first time since security concerns caused the president to leave Turkey on a different aircraft, The Washington Post first reported.

In July, Trump unexpectedly left the NATO summit in Turkey on a different plane , citing a potential threat as the conflict with Iran escalated. He switched to a smaller military aircraft in secret, using a catering truck for deception.

The swap raised further questions about the modified Qatari jet’s security as a presidential aircraft. That same month, Trump announced that the jet would be soon sent to be “maxed out” for security upgrades.

Trump said the alterations would begin in roughly a month, but no official statement has been made about the schedule.

“We don’t comment on specific upgrades or modifications to Air Force One,” a senior administration official told Military Times. “We maintain a consistent posture that ensures a safe, secure, and reliable capability for the President of the United States and routinely evolve the capability as required to maintain that posture.”

Trump will be in Ireland on Sept. 12 and 13, attending the Irish Open at his golf course in Doonbeg. The BBC reported that he is scheduled to meet Irish President Catherine Connolly and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin during his two-day trip.

Ahead of the midterm elections, Trump is also scheduled to headline the Republican midterm convention next week in Texas, and he has promised to campaign for Republican candidates across dozens of battleground states.

items.title: Lost in 1942, WWII Soldier Will Be Laid to Rest in California
items.author: Daniela Vestal
items.summary: The remains of U.S. Army Air Forces Pvt. Lowell C. Akers, 21, who was captured and died as a prisoner of war during World War II, will be interred Sept. 4 in Nevada City, California. Services and internment are being coordinated by Hooper and Weaver Mortuary.
items.body:
FORT KNOX, Ky. – The remains of U.S. Army Air Forces Pvt. Lowell C. Akers, 21, who was captured and died as a prisoner of war during World War II, will be interred Sept. 4 in Nevada City, California. Services and internment are being coordinated by Hooper and Weaver Mortuary. In late 1942, Akers was assigned to First Platoon, 680th Ordnance Company (Aviation Pursuit), when Japanese forces invaded the Philippine Islands in December. Intense fighting continued until the surrender of the Bataan peninsula on April 9, 1942, and of Corregidor Island on May 6, 1942. Thousands of U.S. and Filipino service members were captured and interned at POW camps.Akers was among those reported captured when U.S. forces in Bataan surrendered to the Japanese. They were subjected to the 65-mile Bataan Death March and then held at the Cabanatuan POW Camp #1. More than 2,500 POWs perished in this camp during the war. According to prison camp and other historical records, Akers died of malaria on Nov. 14, 1942, was buried along with other deceased prisoners in the local Cabanatuan Camp Cemetery in Common Grave 723. The Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency accounted for Akers on Sept. 23, 2025. For more information on DPAA’s efforts to locate and identify Akers, please visit: https://www.dpaa.mil/News-Stories/ID-Announcements/Article/4326736/airman-accounted-for-from-world-war-ii-akers-l/ U.S. Army Human Resources Command’s Past Conflict Repatriations Branch plays a vital role in the process of identifying, locating and contacting subsequent generation family members of Soldiers missing or killed in action during WWII and the Korean War to positively identify previously undiscovered or unknown remains. Media interested in covering and/or obtaining more information about the funeral and interment should contact Hooper and Weaver Mortuary, 530-265-2429.

items.title: Space Force May Export Launch Lessons to Foreign Partners
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: As U.S. allies look to establish sovereign military space launch capabilities, the Space Force is exploring ways to transfer lessons learned from its National Security Space Launch program to support its international partners. The post Space Force May Export Launch Lessons to Foreign Partners appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Space Force May Export Launch Lessons to Foreign Partners

Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

As U.S. allies look to establish sovereign military space launch capabilities, the Space Force is exploring ways to transfer lessons learned from its National Security Space Launch program to support its international partners.

In a new notice to industry , issued Sept. 3, the service said it is exploring a specific type of foreign military sales agreement called a technical service case, which involves the U.S. sharing specialized expertise with a foreign partner. The Space Force did not name which country it’s working with but said the nation is interested in acquiring engineering, logistical, and technical assistance to establish their own NSSL-like service using a U.S. commercial launch vehicle, including the spaceport infrastructure to enable it.

The U.S. is the global leader in space launch, conducting nearly 60 percent of all launches worldwide in 2025 , according to analytics and engineering firm BryceTech. The Space Force operates the two busiest U.S. ranges: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Fla., and Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif. Last year, the two spaceports supported 175 launches, and the White House is targeting 1,000 U.S. launches annually by 2030 .

Amid a push from President Donald Trump’s administration for U.S. allies to increase annual spending on defense, some partner nations have announced increases in military space funding—both for space systems and for launch capabilities. In Europe, Germany, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Italy have all funded domestic rocket development. Meanwhile, in April, Canadian lawmakers proposed a regulatory framework for the country to establish its own space launch capabilities after long relying on the U.S. and other countries to reach orbit.

“In a more uncertain and competitive world, Canada cannot rely on others to secure access to space for our economy, our defense, and our future,” Canadian Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon, who introduced the Canadian Space Launch Act, said in an April 21 statement . “Establishing Canadian sovereign space launch capabilities would drive billions in investments, create good paying jobs, increase Canada’s sovereignty, reduce our economy’s reliance on the United States, and support a commercial space launch and re-entry industry that could be worth $40 billion.”

To support the FMS request, the Space Force is looking to select a contractor to help tailor U.S. best practices in launch and spaceport operations for the country’s specific requirements, and evaluate whether certain commercial launch vehicles and spaceport operators are a good fit for its needs. The contractor will also recommend a mission assurance approach for the country, based on its needs. The company will work with Space Systems Command’s portfolio acquisition executive for space access to compile data and craft a report on its findings.

The Space Force expects to award a contract by Sept. 25 and compile the report within 12 months.

As USSF helps its partners grow their sovereign launch capabilities, it’s also considering options to launch its own payloads from foreign soil . While this effort doesn’t address that, officials have said there could be opportunities to partner with Australia, New Zealand, Japan, and countries in Europe, but there are U.S. policy hurdles that need to be addressed first.
